1200-chophouse.text: Chef-owner Dan Casey started on the beach with a hot dog stand, Dan's Beachside, on July 4, 1986 ($86 in sales the first day), moved on to Snapper's Sea Grill in 1998, and then built this steakhouse in a restored Old Florida beach house on the Intracoastal. The name is the temperature of the broiler that sears the steaks; his son Connor now runs the place.
1200-chophouse.descriptor: Upscale steakhouse in an old beach house on Gulf Blvd, St. Pete Beach

3-daughters-brewing.text: Started in December 2013 by restaurateurs Mike and Leigh Harting (with chef Ty Weaver) after a house-brewed beer created for a beer-battered dish at their restaurant Bella Brava took off on tap. The name came from Leigh asking how many beers they'd have to sell to put their three daughters through college; the tasting room on 22nd St S is now billed as one of Florida's busiest, and Beach Blonde Ale is the signature beer.
3-daughters-brewing.descriptor: Large brewery and tasting room on 22nd St S since 2013

9-bangkok-thai-restaurant.text: Owner Yui Chaisurivirat, who came to St. Pete from Thailand in 1985 after running Asian-fusion spots in Lakeland and Orlando, opened 9 Bangkok on the 500 block of Central around 2001, making it one of Central Avenue's original spots. Regulars come for the duck curry, pad Thai, noodle soup and sushi.
9-bangkok-thai-restaurant.descriptor: Thai and sushi spot at 571 Central Ave downtown, open since about 2001

abc-chinese-seafood.descriptor: Chinese restaurant at 2705 54th Ave N in Lealman

agave.text: Opened around 2003 by a couple who started out as a server and a cook, Agave serves the northern-central Mexican recipes she learned from her father in La Comarca Lagunera; nearly the whole staff is family, and the egg-battered chile relleno topped with pomegranate is the signature dish.
agave.descriptor: Family-run northern Mexican restaurant on Gulf Blvd in St. Pete Beach, since ~2003

al-lang-stadium.text: Built in 1947 and named for the ex-mayor who lured spring training to St. Pete, this waterfront ballpark hosted the Cardinals (1948–97), Yankees, Mets and finally the Devil Rays until the last spring game in 2008. The grandstand faces the harbor so nearly every seat looks out on Tampa Bay; since 2011 it has been the soccer-only home of the Tampa Bay Rowdies.
al-lang-stadium.descriptor: Waterfront stadium downtown, home pitch of the Tampa Bay Rowdies

albert-whitted-park.text: Opened in 2008 on the north edge of the airport, with observation spots for watching planes land a few yards away and an airplane-themed playground. Both park and airport honor James Albert Whitted, a St. Pete native and one of the Navy's first 250 aviators, who died when the propeller broke off his seaplane Falcon near Pensacola. In 2003, voters overwhelmingly chose to keep the airport rather than turn it all into parkland.
albert-whitted-park.descriptor: Waterfront park with an airplane-themed playground beside the downtown airport

athenian-garden.text: A family-owned Greek restaurant established in 1977, Athenian Garden now runs two St. Pete locations, this one on 4th St N and another in Tyrone; it used to sit in the old Coconut Grove plaza (now a Fresh Market). Inside, Grecian murals cover the walls and the saganaki cheese is flamed with brandy and lemon.
athenian-garden.descriptor: Family-owned Greek restaurant on 4th St N, established 1977

azalea-park.text: A 35-acre city park in the Tyrone area of west St. Pete, wrapped around the Azalea Recreation Center and its sports complex; in 2001 the center added Richard Medlock's public artwork "Poetic Environment." In 2025 the park became the western end of the city's Lime e-bike-share expansion, letting riders pedal from downtown all the way to 72nd St N.
azalea-park.descriptor: 35-acre neighborhood park with a rec center and sports complex on 72nd St N

baba.text: George and Debbie Sayegh, the couple behind Bodega, opened Baba in June 2019 as a Greek-Lebanese restaurant named for their fathers: baba means dad in both languages. In 2023 they added Barbouni, a nine-seat sister spot. Both closed after service on July 3, 2026, with longtime team members reopening the space as Barra Barra and Kaixo.
baba.descriptor: Greek-Lebanese restaurant at 2701 Central in the Grand Central District (2019-2026)

banana-hammock.text: An open-air tiki-style bar inside the Five Bucks Drinkery complex on the 200 block of Central, sharing space with The Garden, with a 10,000-square-foot patio, all-day happy hour and 32-ounce frozen drinks; the namesake cocktail mixes coconut rum, banana liqueur, crème de cacao and amaretto shaken with whipped cream.
banana-hammock.descriptor: Outdoor tiki-style patio bar with frozen drinks at 247 Central Ave

bandit-coffee.text: Joshua and Sarah Weaver opened Bandit in 2016 inside a former Porter's Paints store in the Grand Central District, and by 2020 they were roasting their own beans at a facility off 7th Avenue South. The shop famously has no WiFi on purpose — the owners say it's there for good food and good drinks with good company, not laptops.
bandit-coffee.descriptor: Minimalist roastery café on Central Ave in Grand Central, since 2016

bavaros.text: Bavaro's began in Tampa in March 2009 as what it calls Florida's first traditional Neapolitan pizzeria, after founder Dan Bavaro moved his family down from New Jersey. Pies come out of hand-built wood-fired brick ovens running around 900°F, made with a 100-year-old yeast culture and century-old family recipes; this Central Avenue spot is the group's St. Pete outpost in the Edge District.
bavaros.descriptor: Wood-fired Neapolitan pizza and fresh pasta on Central Ave in the Edge District

bella-brava.text: Born from the owners' 2003 trip through Tuscany, BellaBrava opened in 2005 on Central Avenue and moved to its Beach Drive patio spot in 2010. It's a scratch kitchen that makes its pasta, pizza dough and focaccia daily and fires pizzas in wood-burning Woodstone ovens; the same group later opened Stillwaters Tavern up the street.
bella-brava.descriptor: Tuscan-inspired Italian restaurant with wood-fired pizza on Beach Drive since 2010

black-crow-coffee.text: Owner-roaster Greg Bauman, a Toronto native who got hooked on coffee at Jet Fuel on Parliament Street, opened his first shop in Indian Shores in 2007 and started roasting in St. Pete in 2016 — the single-origin beans are roasted right at this Grand Central location and sold in compostable one-pound bags. A second Black Crow sits in the Old Northeast on 2nd St N.
black-crow-coffee.descriptor: Indie coffee shop and in-house roaster at 2161 1st Ave S

writtenFor.name: Black Crow Coffee - Grand Central District

blue-fugu.descriptor: Japanese hibachi-and-sushi eatery on Gulf Blvd in St. Pete Beach

bodega.text: Opened in 2013 by Brooklyn transplants George and Debbie Sayegh as a tiny walk-up window at 10th and Central, Bodega built its reputation on pressed Cuban sandwiches made with bread from Tampa's Casino Bakery, with lines around the block on Friday nights. It moved a block west to this larger space at 1180 Central in 2019 and added the Bar Chica speakeasy in back.
bodega.descriptor: Cuban sandwich counter in the EDGE District since 2013

boulevard-burgers-and-tap-house.text: Beach-town burger joint at 5905 Gulf Blvd known for its over-the-top builds: the ultra-spicy Ghost Rider and the Haystack, piled high with skinny onion rings. Full liquor bar with local craft brews, a pool table and live music on weekends.
boulevard-burgers-and-tap-house.descriptor: Burger and craft-beer bar on Gulf Blvd in St. Pete Beach

boyd-hill-nature-preserve.text: The city bought the Lake Maggiore shoreline in 1943, began building the nature trail in 1947, and renamed it in 1958 for Boyd Hill, the parks superintendent who supervised its trails and plantings and died in 1957. Today it's about 245 acres of pine flatwoods, scrub and swamp on Lake Maggiore, with 3+ miles of trails, a raptor aviary and metal wildlife sculptures by local artist Paul Eppling.
boyd-hill-nature-preserve.descriptor: 245-acre nature preserve with trails and a raptor aviary on Lake Maggiore

brick-mortar.text: Chef Jason Ruhe and Hope Montgomery ran In Bloom Catering for nearly a decade before opening this 500-block dining room in April 2015 — the name is a nod to finally having a real dining room of their own. The rustic room cures its own salmon, makes its own pasta and pickles, and the couple went on to open Seaworthy Fish + Bar and Pulpo Kitchen + Lounge.
brick-mortar.descriptor: Rustic farm-to-table dining room on the 500 block of Central Ave since 2015

brooklyn-south.text: A tiny mom-and-pop cheese, charcuterie and sandwich shop that has anchored the Edge District since about 2014. It changed hands in 2020 but kept its cheesemonger and a 40-plus sandwich menu; the Italian and the Cuban are the top sellers, and it doubles as a wine-and-cheese stop.
brooklyn-south.descriptor: Mom-and-pop deli and cheese shop at 1437 Central Ave in the Edge District

buona-ristorante.text: Open since January 2008 and run by Diane and Marco Angelo since 2017, it's known locally for the busy pizza take-out counter up front and a hidden back patio that looks onto a small marina on Boca Ciega Bay.
buona-ristorante.descriptor: Family-owned Italian & pizza spot in Dolphin Village plaza, St. Pete Beach

burger-monger.text: A Tampa-born burger chain (founded 2010) that brought its Akaushi-beef burgers, beef-tallow fries and Häagen-Dazs shakes to 4th Street North in 2016. In 2024 the St. Pete location expanded into a full liquor bar with games and a stage for trivia, karaoke and live music.
burger-monger.descriptor: Tampa-born Akaushi-beef burger joint on 4th St N, in St. Pete since 2016

caddys-on-the-beach.text: Caddy's has been a Sunset Beach hangout since the 1940s and bills itself as the only beach bar directly on the sand where you can drink a cocktail with your feet in the sand. Hurricanes Helene and Milton buried its ground floor under three to four feet of sand in 2024; the crew served from a tent and food truck for about 18 months until the rebuilt bar reopened in April 2026.
caddys-on-the-beach.descriptor: Toes-in-the-sand beach bar on Sunset Beach, Treasure Island, since the 1940s

cafe-gala.text: The Dalí Museum's café is named for Salvador Dalí's wife and muse, Gala, and the menu leans Spanish to match — tapas, gazpacho, caldo gallego, crema catalana and mantecado cookies, with locally roasted Kahwa coffee and cava rosado to drink. Tables spill out onto the museum's Avant-garden patio.
cafe-gala.descriptor: Spanish tapas cafe inside the Dali Museum, with a patio on the Avant-garden

cafe-soleil-french-bakery-deli.text: Owner Lauren Chezaud moved here from Paris and opened this St. Pete Beach bakery because, she says, she couldn't survive without good coffee and bread. It's known for thirteen kinds of toasted croissants (house-made croissants pressed panini-style), and in 2023 it moved up Gulf Blvd into a space three times the size of the original.
cafe-soleil-french-bakery-deli.descriptor: French bakery and deli on Gulf Blvd in St. Pete Beach, known for toasted croissants

cage-brewing.text: Dead Set Florida is known locally as 'the band that saved The Cage': bassist Christian Walker, now a co-owner, and keyboardist Tucker Waud took over what I Love the Burg called 'a pile of dirt with a flea market inside,' laid turf over it and built out a family-friendly music yard with murals, an octopus sculpture and an oak-fired pizza oven. Nightly live music and multi-day fests like Heat Fest are the house specialty.
cage-brewing.descriptor: Microbrewery, pizzeria and live-music beer yard at 2001 1st Ave S

cali.text: Opened around 2005 as Ciccio Cali by Tampa's Ciccio Restaurant Group, this 37th Avenue spot just off 4th Street brought the group's 'Real Food Only' California-style menu to St. Pete long before the healthy-fast-casual wave.
cali.descriptor: California-style 'Real Food Only' restaurant just off 4th St N; Ciccio Restaurant Group

cappys-pizza.text: A St. Pete staple at 2900 1st Ave N that has been bringing Chicago-style deep dish to the Bay since 1995 — iron-skillet pies with a dense, focaccia-like crust — alongside New York-style pizza, calzones, and a brick patio out front.
cappys-pizza.descriptor: Chicago deep-dish and New York-style pizzeria at 2900 1st Ave N since 1995

carmelitas-mexican-restaurant.text: Carmelita's began in 1983 as a nine-booth spot on Park St N run by Carmen and Vincent Lopez on their family recipes; this 66th Street location opened in 1994 as the second one. Juan and Maria Guzman, who started in the original kitchen in the early '80s and rose to head cook and kitchen manager, bought this branch in 2008 and run it with their kids.
carmelitas-mexican-restaurant.descriptor: Family-run Mexican restaurant at 66th St & 62nd Ave N, Pinellas Park, since 1994

carmelitas-mexican-restaurant-park-stree.text: This Park Street spot is the original Carmelita's, opened in 1983 by Carmen and Vincent Lopez with just nine booths and their family recipes. The Lopez family still runs it, and the restaurant has since grown to five locations around Pinellas County.
carmelitas-mexican-restaurant-park-stree.descriptor: Family-run Mexican restaurant on Park St N, the original since 1983

writtenFor.name: Carmelita's Mexican Restaurant - Park Street North

casita-taqueria.text: Don and Gwen Arvin left corporate jobs to open Casita in 2011, inspired by the tacos they ate on West Coast trips. The original 4th Street shop had to move to Central Avenue when Trader Joe's took over its plaza in 2014, and the taqueria has since grown to four locations, including this return to 4th Street, all pressing corn tortillas in-house daily.
casita-taqueria.descriptor: Locally owned taqueria with house-made corn tortillas on 4th St N; since 2011

casita-taqueria-historic-kenwood.text: Don and Gwen Arvin, ex-corporate refugees, opened Casita in 2011 modeled on the hole-in-the-wall taquerias they'd found on trips through California and Oregon; in 2014 it moved into this 1935 former Texaco station on Central Ave, with a dog-friendly patio out front. Corn tortillas, salsas and guac are all made in-house.
casita-taqueria-historic-kenwood.descriptor: Taqueria in a 1935 ex-Texaco station on Central Ave, since 2014

casita-taqueria-holiday-park.text: The third outpost of Don and Gwen Arvin's homegrown taqueria, slated to open in the Tyrone area in January 2019 with help from the Vitale Bros. Like the originals, the corn tortillas are pressed in-house and the meats slow-braised; the ancho-marinated cod fish tacos are the calling card.
casita-taqueria-holiday-park.descriptor: Local taqueria with house-made corn tortillas on 66th St N, third location

cassis.text: Philippe Berriot, a Le Bec-Fin alum, and architect Lisa Wannemacher opened this French-American brasserie on Beach Drive in spring 2010, years before the new Pier turned the waterfront into a tourist draw; an in-house bakery followed within months and Cassis Market in 2011.
cassis.descriptor: French-American brasserie on Beach Drive NE since 2010, with an in-house bakery

cassis-american-brasserie.text: Philippe Berriot, a Le Bec-Fin alum, and architect Lisa Wannemacher opened this French-American brasserie on Beach Drive in spring 2010, years before the new Pier turned the waterfront into a tourist draw; an in-house bakery followed within months and Cassis Market in 2011.
cassis-american-brasserie.descriptor: French-American brasserie on Beach Drive NE since 2010, with an in-house bakery

casual-clam.text: Self-billed as 'Everyone's Favorite Clam Shack,' this MLK Street spot has served New England-style seafood since 1991 — whole-belly Ipswich clams, a clam chowder made fresh daily, and lobster rolls — from a picnic-bench patio painted with colorful murals.
casual-clam.descriptor: New England-style clam shack on MLK St N since 1991

central-diner.text: It opened on March 5, 1975 as the Central Coffee Shoppe and has been a downtown breakfast spot ever since, now family-owned under the Central Diner name with cozy booths, John's Special blueberry pancakes and country fried steak.
central-diner.descriptor: Family-owned breakfast-and-lunch diner at 530 Central Ave, open since 1975

central-pizza-subs.descriptor: Independent neighborhood pizza and sub shop at 6405 Central Ave N

ceviche-tapas-bar.text: A Beach Drive fixture since 1997, this Barcelona-inspired tapas-and-paella house later moved from its corner spot up the street into the former Moon Under Water space. Locals will tell you the sangria has been a staple for more than two decades.
ceviche-tapas-bar.descriptor: Spanish tapas and paella bar on Beach Drive NE since 1997

chihuly-collection.text: The Morean Arts Center partnered with Dale Chihuly in 2010 to bring his glass to St. Pete on Beach Drive, then moved the collection in August 2016 to this building at 720 Central Ave, billed as the first installation of Chihuly's art in a building designed specifically for that purpose. A ticket includes a live glassblowing demo at the Morean Glass Studio around the corner.
chihuly-collection.descriptor: Dedicated Dale Chihuly glass-art gallery on the 700 block of Central Ave

chile-verde.descriptor: Neighborhood Mexican restaurant on 22nd Ave N with weekend pozole and menudo

chill-restaurant-bar.descriptor: American-fusion brunch, lunch and dinner spot with live music on Corey Avenue

clam-bayou-nature-preserve.text: A pocket of wild Boca Ciega Bay shoreline on the Gulfport–St. Pete line, part of a 170-acre estuary once called Osgood Point. A 1995 restoration replanted native vegetation and built the boardwalks; a 2010–11 project cleaned up the stormwater flowing into the bay. Paddlers launch here for a mangrove tunnel, and spoonbills, fiddler crabs, dolphins and manatees turn up.
clam-bayou-nature-preserve.descriptor: Mangrove estuary preserve with boardwalks and a kayak launch on Boca Ciega Bay

cocktail-st-pete.text: Opened May 7, 2021 by David Fischer, the nightlife owner behind Zazoo'd and The Saint speakeasy on the same Grand Central block, under the motto "Stiff Drinks, Hard Liquor, Raging Good Times." Built around a circular bar with a pool bar out back (The Wet Spot), it has stacked up Best of the Bay wins for LGBTQ bar and dance club, and TLC filmed an episode of Welcome to Plathville there.
cocktail-st-pete.descriptor: LGBTQ+ cocktail and dance bar in the Grand Central District, open since 2021

coconut-charlies-beach-bar.text: A long-time favorite beach bar right on the sand at 6100 Gulf Blvd in St. Pete Beach, known for some of the best bar food on the beach; it reopened with revamped digs after the 2024 hurricanes and opened a second outpost with a tiki-hut beach bar inside the DoubleTree resort in North Redington Beach in early 2024.
coconut-charlies-beach-bar.descriptor: Beachfront bar and grill at 6100 Gulf Blvd, St. Pete Beach

copa.text: Opened in November 2019 by St. Pete-raised brothers Maxim and Sebastien Thuriere, who built the Afro-Latin Caribbean menu around their Haitian and French Caribbean roots. It survived opening just months before the pandemic to become an Edge District staple, known for craft cocktails and Sunday Latin jazz; sister spot Café COPA opened next door in 2024.
copa.descriptor: Afro-Latin Caribbean fusion restaurant and cocktail bar in the Edge District since 2019

copper-shaker.text: Opened in spring 2017 at 169 1st Ave N by Jeremy Wallace and Jeff Catherell, the pair behind Cask & Ale, Copper Shaker is a downtown craft-cocktail bar and kitchen stocking 700-plus spirits and 200-plus whiskies and pouring until 3 a.m.
copper-shaker.descriptor: Craft cocktail bar and kitchen on 1st Ave N downtown, open until 3 a.m.

crab-shack.descriptor: No-frills Gandy Blvd seafood house serving crab claws, blue crab, frog legs and gator

crabby-bills.text: The St. Pete Beach outpost of the Loder family's Crabby Bill's, opened in 1993 a decade after the original in Indian Rocks Beach. The Loders had been selling blue crabs, fish and clams around Florida since settling in Madeira Beach in 1968; daughter Eleanor reportedly named the business with the line 'Dad is crabby, we like crabs, why not Crabby Bill's?' After a 1998 fire the restaurant was rebuilt with a tiki bar and a rooftop deck for Gulf sunsets.
crabby-bills.descriptor: Beachfront seafood house on Gulf Blvd with a rooftop tiki bar, since 1993

craft-kafe.text: St. Pete's dedicated gluten-free bakery-cafe, opened February 2015 at 6653 Central Ave by Teddy Skiadiotis, who got his start at his father's St. Pete Beach restaurant, Skidder's. The whole concept started with a regular named June, a celiac customer he baked a gluten-free pizza for; the giant cinnamon rolls it's now famous for came out of a botched batch of sausage rolls. The founder's vision included a stone mill to make fresh flour in-house.
craft-kafe.descriptor: Dedicated gluten-free bakery-cafe on Central Ave at 66th St, since 2015

writtenFor.name: Craft Kafe - Pasadena On The Gulf

craft-kafe-dtsp.text: The downtown outpost of a fully gluten-free bakery and café founded in March 2015 by Teddy Skiadiotis, a former Wall Street trader whose family ran Skidders on St. Pete Beach for 30 years. The 200 Central space opened in March 2018 after more than a year of delays, in a corner spot where several earlier restaurants and bars had been short-lived; the bakery even builds its own flour blends.
craft-kafe-dtsp.descriptor: Downtown branch of a 100% gluten-free bakery-café at 200 Central Ave, since 2018

crescent-lake-park.text: The park dates to the 1920s, when developer Perry Snell held the land until the city could buy it; its south-end ballfield became the Yankees' spring-training practice ground from 1925, hosting Ruth, Gehrig and DiMaggio, then the first Mets camp under Casey Stengel in 1962, and was added to the National Register in 2019. Legend says Babe Ruth refused to shag fly balls there because alligators sunned on the lake bank that formed part of the outfield.
crescent-lake-park.descriptor: Lakeside city park north of downtown with a dog park and the historic Huggins-Stengel Field

da-sesto-italiano-ristorante-e-vino.text: Chef Sesto, a mechanical engineer who sold pasta-making equipment in Italy, moved his family to St. Petersburg in 1997 after acquiring the Florida Pasta Company, then opened Da Sesto in January 2007; it later outgrew its space and moved to 66th Street North in Pinellas Park, where handmade pasta and the 'Mamma Angela' recipe are the house signatures.
da-sesto-italiano-ristorante-e-vino.descriptor: Italian trattoria with handmade pasta at 7201 66th St N, Pinellas Park

writtenFor.name: Da Sesto Italiano Ristorante e Vino

dead-bobs.text: Named for a real Bob, a larger-than-life party regular the owners met at a Miami Beach pool bar and who died in 2013 shortly after they reconnected. Ben Scherlis's dive bar spent 11 years at 6716 Central before moving a few blocks east into the old Kay's Family Restaurant in late 2025, keeping the 3 a.m. hours, 25 TVs and cheap burgers, wings and Philly egg rolls that made it a west St. Pete institution.
dead-bobs.descriptor: Late-night dive bar and burger joint at 6475 Central Ave in west St. Pete

demens-landing-park.text: Named for Peter Demens, the Russian-born railroad man who brought the Orange Belt Railway to town in 1888 and — legend says after winning a coin toss with his partner John C. Williams — named the new city after his hometown of St. Petersburg. Today it's the downtown waterfront park on Bayboro Harbor beside the Municipal Marina, home to the city's sailing center.

dooriban.descriptor: Korean homestyle restaurant at 5600 66th St N

driftwood-kava-roastery-st-pete.descriptor: Late-night kava bar and in-house coffee roastery on the 700 block of Central Ave

duncan-mcclellan-gallery.text: Glass artist Duncan McClellan converted a 7,800-square-foot former fish-and-tomato packing plant into a gallery, sculpture garden and working hot shop around 2009, becoming one of the first tenants of what grew into the Warehouse Arts District. It shows dozens of glass artists from around the world and runs the DMG School Project, which brings glassblowing to local schoolkids.
duncan-mcclellan-gallery.descriptor: Glass-art gallery and hot shop in an old packing plant, Warehouse Arts District

el-cap.text: A 1948 pub renamed El Cap in 1958 by an owner who gave all his bars baseball-cap names, it became a sandwich shop when Pennsylvania transplants Steve and Rose Bonfili bought it in 1963. Their son Frank plastered the walls with baseball memorabilia in the 1980s, making it arguably St. Pete's first sports bar; one prep cook has hand-formed patties here since 1992 and claims over two million burgers.
el-cap.descriptor: Old-school burger and beer joint on 4th St N, in the same family for decades

emerald-bar.text: Opened by the Marano family in 1950 three blocks up Central and moved to this spot in 1964, the Emerald is one of the oldest continuously running bars in St. Pete. It's a no-frills dive that hosts live music and art shows, and it's still a smoking bar.
emerald-bar.descriptor: Family-owned dive bar at 550 Central Ave since 1964, founded 1950

engine-no-9.text: Chef Jason Esposito opened this burger bar in September 2012; the red building reminded him of a firehouse and he'd just heard the song 'Engine Engine No. 9,' so the name stuck. Esposito is hockey royalty — dad Tony and uncle Phil are Hall of Famers who helped found the Lightning — which is why it's wall-to-wall hockey and bills itself as the only Chicago Blackhawks bar outside Chicago.
engine-no-9.descriptor: Hockey-themed gourmet burger bar in the Edge District since 2012

fabrica-pizza.text: Fabrica started in Tampa's Channel District in 2015 and opened its downtown St. Pete shop in 2017, serving thin, slightly crunchy-crusted pies. The Italian guide 50 Top Pizza listed it among the top 50 US pizzerias in 2022, then ranked it the 15th best pizzeria in the United States (and 97th in the world) in 2023.
fabrica-pizza.descriptor: Downtown St. Pete outpost of a Tampa-born pizzeria, since 2017

fergs-sports-bar-grill.text: Mark Ferguson, a Pinellas County schoolteacher who admits he had no business opening a bar, launched Ferg's in 1992 in a converted Sunoco gas station in the old Gas Plant District, on a stretch of Central Avenue with little going for it beyond cheap land. When the Rays began play at Tropicana Field in 1998 it became the game-day front porch, linked to the stadium property by a tunnel under 1st Avenue South, and has sprawled to nearly two city blocks with 90-plus TVs.
fergs-sports-bar-grill.descriptor: Sprawling sports bar across from Tropicana Field on Central Ave, since 1992

five-bucks-drinkery.text: The second outpost of a bar that's been a staple of downtown St. Pete's 200 block of Central Ave, this Pinellas Park location opened June 15, 2023 at 7402 49th St N with off-street parking and more elbow room. The signature move is a 32-ounce Long Island Iced Tea served in a wonton-soup cup.
five-bucks-drinkery.descriptor: Restaurant and bar on 49th St N, Pinellas Park outpost of a downtown St. Pete bar

five-bucks-drinkery-downtown.text: A locally owned fixture of the 200 block of Central Avenue for more than a decade, Five Bucks is where a lot of downtown First Fridays start and weekends end. It's known for oversized drinks, including 32-ounce Long Island Iced Teas served in wonton soup cups, and it grew into Pinellas Park (2023) and Seminole spinoffs.
five-bucks-drinkery-downtown.descriptor: Cheap-drinks sports bar and grill on the 200 block of Central Ave for over a decade

flamingo-sports-bar.text: Jack Kerouac spent his last months in 1969 drinking here from a corner stool that let him watch every door; owner Dale Nichols, who bought the bar that year, says he may have poured Kerouac's last drink before the writer died on October 21. The building goes back to 1923 as a beer-joint barbecue, and legend says Yankees pitcher Johnny Allen, a friend of Ruth and Gehrig, added onto it in the 1930s while training nearby.
flamingo-sports-bar.descriptor: Old-school pool hall and dive on MLK St N, a St. Pete bar since 1923

flippers-pizzeria.text: Flippers began in 1987 when three college friends opened an 895-square-foot shop near Orlando's convention center; it has since grown into a chain of restaurants across Florida. Every store still makes its dough in-house with a 96-plus-hour cold ferment and bakes in high-temperature brick ovens.
flippers-pizzeria.descriptor: Florida craft-pizza chain's brick-oven shop at 1054 4th St N

florida-holocaust-museum.text: Founded in 1992 by Walter and Edith Loebenberg, who fled Nazi Germany, it moved downtown in 1998 with Elie Wiesel cutting the ribbon and is one of the largest Holocaust museums in the country. Its centerpiece is boxcar #113 069-5, a German railcar used to carry victims to the camps, resting on rails from the Treblinka killing center.
florida-holocaust-museum.descriptor: Holocaust history museum on 5th St S, downtown, one of the largest in the US

floridian-social-club.text: Built in 1924 as the Alexander National Bank, the Beaux Arts building became the single-screen State Theatre in 1950 and later a concert club that hosted They Might Be Giants, Fall Out Boy and Twenty One Pilots. Fire-code violations shut it in 2017; Kevin Chadwick bought it and reopened it in February 2021 as the Floridian Social Club, now mostly a wedding and event venue.
floridian-social-club.descriptor: Restored 1920s bank turned State Theatre, now an event and music venue on Central Ave

fort-de-soto-county-park.text: A 1,100-plus-acre county park spread across five keys at the mouth of Tampa Bay, built around a Spanish-American War fort begun in 1898 whose 12-inch mortar battery never saw combat. North Beach was named America's Best Beach by Dr. Beach in 2005, and the park has a 236-site campground, a dog beach and a ferry to Egmont Key.
fort-de-soto-county-park.descriptor: Five-key county park with an 1898 fort, campground and Gulf beaches

fortu.text: Restaurateur Shan Bakrac (Top Slice, Black Cattle Burgers) spent two years building this elevated Pan-Asian restaurant and steakhouse, opening December 5, 2023 in the long-vacant former Ceviche space at the Ponce de Leon Hotel on Central Ave and Beach Drive. Wagyu, oxtail gyoza and wagyu wonton tacos anchor a shareable-plates menu backed by a deep sake list; a sister izakaya, ISU, opened beneath it in 2025.
fortu.descriptor: Upscale Pan-Asian restaurant and steakhouse in the Ponce de Leon Hotel downtown

fortunatos-italian-pizzeria-northeast.text: The Fortunato's name has bounced around town: an earlier Fortunato's on Central Avenue downtown drew lines of Eckerd students and First Friday crowds for its thick slices, then resurfaced on Beach Boulevard in Gulfport before this Northeast Shopping Plaza shop opened in December 2021. Its calling card is a 16-inch deep-dish Sicilian pizza, served under a mural by the Vitale Bros.
fortunatos-italian-pizzeria-northeast.descriptor: Deep-dish Sicilian and NY-slice pizzeria in Northeast Shopping Plaza, since 2021

fortunatos-italian-pizzeria-pasadena.text: One of the Fortunato's pizzerias run by Vinny Fortunato, who told the Gabber in 2019 he has opened 34 restaurants since 1976 and makes everything fresh daily — bread, sauce, dressings. The original downtown spot at 259 Central Ave gave way to the Crafty Squirrel in 2018.
fortunatos-italian-pizzeria-pasadena.descriptor: Family-run Italian pizzeria on Gulfport Blvd S at Pasadena Ave

fourth-street-shrimp-store.text: The building went up in 1928 as a Model T service station, later became a laundromat with a little seafood market tucked inside, and that market started frying shrimp baskets and grouper sandwiches in 1984. The Shrimp Store outgrew the space and expanded in 1997.
fourth-street-shrimp-store.descriptor: Fried-shrimp and grouper joint in a 1928 ex-gas station on 4th St N, since 1984

frays-donut-house.text: A 'Burg institution since 1993 housed in groovy retro buildings with drive-thrus; each Fray's shop has its own owner, but the donuts are made fresh overnight for a 5:30 a.m. open, and the cronuts and sausage rolls routinely sell out early. Unsold donuts get donated to a local church.
frays-donut-house.descriptor: Old-school 5:30 a.m. donut shop; a St. Pete institution since 1993

frays-donut-house-historic-kenwood.text: The Fray's name has been a St. Pete donut fixture since 1993, known for strong coffee, super-sweet glazed rings and heavily sprinkled signature donuts. The 34th Street shop in Historic Kenwood is one of several around town; the shops share a name and old-school hand-made style, but not every one is under the same owner.
frays-donut-house-historic-kenwood.descriptor: Old-school hand-made donut shop on 34th St N in Historic Kenwood

frescos-waterfront-bistro.text: Attorney David Sockol bought a small marina restaurant called Apropos in 2003, renamed it Fresco's and built a deck out over the water at the entrance to the St. Pete Pier. Billed as the longest continuously running restaurant on Beach Drive, it sits on city-owned land at the Municipal Marina, and the city's marina redevelopment plan envisions demolishing and replacing the building, citing degraded seawalls.
frescos-waterfront-bistro.descriptor: Casual waterfront seafood spot at the Municipal Marina by the St. Pete Pier

gigis-italian-restaurants.text: Open since 1967, this family-run trattoria is a Treasure Island staple, known for Old World flavors and imported pasta.
gigis-italian-restaurants.descriptor: Family-run Italian trattoria in Treasure Island since 1967

glory-days-grill.text: Glory Days is a Virginia-born sports bar chain founded in 1996 in Burke, VA; in 2023 its Florida franchise owner, Outback Steakhouse co-founder Bob Basham, bought out the 22 mid-Atlantic restaurants, bringing the whole brand under one owner. The Tyrone location sponsors a stack of local school and Little League teams.
glory-days-grill.descriptor: Sports bar chain at Tyrone (4088 Park St N), wings, fish fry and a 24oz margarita

good-night-john-boy.text: A 4,000-square-foot 1970s disco bar on the Jannus Block that opened April 27, 2023, complete with a lit-up tiled dance floor, mirror balls and a giant Farrah Fawcett poster. It's the St. Pete outpost of a Cleveland-born concept, and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers shot their 2023 Creamsicle throwback-uniform reveal video here with Derrick Brooks, Ronde Barber and Mike Alstott.
good-night-john-boy.descriptor: '70s disco-themed nightclub on the Jannus Block at 16 2nd St N, opened 2023

grand-hacienda.text: Owner Claudia Johnson grew up in Mexico City cooking alongside her grandmother, moved to Tampa Bay for a business job, and started out baking desserts for other restaurants from home before opening her first Mexican restaurant in Sarasota in 2007. Grand Hacienda is one of seven she now runs; the decor was imported from Mexico.
grand-hacienda.descriptor: Mexican restaurant, one of seven Tampa Bay spots run by owner Claudia Johnson

grazzi.text: Owner Tony Mangiafico has run Gratzzi downtown for more than two decades, and the 'Bada Bing' is the house signature. When the pandemic shut the city down in March 2020, the kitchen started serving free daily lunches to laid-off hospitality workers on March 18 and passed 500 meals within weeks.
grazzi.descriptor: Family-run Italian grille at 2nd St S & 2nd Ave S, downtown since ~1999

great-explorations-childrens-museum.text: Founded in 1986 by the Junior League of St. Petersburg and Hands-On Inc., the museum's original downtown home featured a 90-foot, completely blacked-out Touch Tunnel that kids navigated by feel. It later moved next door to the refurbished Sunken Gardens on 4th Street North, dropped the 'Hands-On' name, and became the first mid-sized children's museum in the country to earn American Alliance of Museums accreditation.
great-explorations-childrens-museum.descriptor: Hands-on children's museum next to Sunken Gardens on 4th St N

green-bench-brewing-co.text: St. Pete's first microbrewery, opened in 2013 by Khris Johnson, Nathan Stonecipher and Steven Duffy after they got the city to change its zoning rules. The name reclaims the thousands of hunter-green benches that earned St. Pete its 'City of Green Benches' nickname from 1916 on — benches Black residents were barred from using under Jim Crow — and Johnson is recognized as Florida's first Black brewery owner. Its Webb's City Cellar barrel house earned a James Beard semifinalist nod.
green-bench-brewing-co.descriptor: St. Pete's first microbrewery with a big beer garden, on Baum Ave since 2013

grove-surf-coffee.text: Hurricane Helene put 34 inches of water through this surf shop-cafe in 2024, and owners Lindsey and Peter Gottschling kept going through their Indian Rocks Beach sister cafe until they reopened here after 256 days, in June 2025, just in time for the shop's fifth birthday. The toasted coconut latte is a local favorite.
grove-surf-coffee.descriptor: Surf shop and specialty coffee bar on Gulf Blvd, St. Pete Beach, since 2020

hangar-restaurant-and-flight-lounge.text: Since April 2010 this second-floor terminal restaurant at Albert Whitted Airport has let diners watch private planes land on the airfield. The airfield is named for James Albert Whitted, a St. Pete native and one of the Navy's pioneering aviators, and sits steps from the yacht basin where Tony Jannus flew the world's first scheduled commercial airline flight on New Year's Day 1914. Longtime head chef Matt Smith bought the place in 2022.
hangar-restaurant-and-flight-lounge.descriptor: Airport-terminal restaurant overlooking Albert Whitted's runway, since 2010

harrys-beach-bar.text: Opened in 1983, Harry's is the oldest beach bar on St. Pete Beach and is named for Harry Nicklaus, one of the original owners of the Sirata, the resort that has stood on this stretch of sand since the 1960s. The resort sold for $207 million in December 2022 to Kentucky-based Columbia Sussex, but Harry's still pours under the same name.
harrys-beach-bar.descriptor: Beachfront resort bar at the Sirata (5300 Gulf Blvd) since 1983, fire pit and live music

hawkers-asian-street-food.text: Four friends who started Hawkers on Mills Avenue in Orlando in 2011, after Thanksgiving potlucks of their families' Asian comfort food, opened this EDGE District outpost in March 2016; about half the menu comes from those handed-down recipes, with roti canai the signature.
hawkers-asian-street-food.descriptor: Pan-Asian street-food restaurant in the EDGE District, known for roti canai

hooks-sushi.text: Founder Hook Atsavinh was an irrepressibly gregarious character and a first-class sushi chef whose motto was "All fish and no bull." He died suddenly in 2009 at age 44, but the restaurant carried on and still bears his name, serving recipes he brought from Thailand, Japan, Korea and China.
hooks-sushi.descriptor: Sushi and Thai spot at 1210 9th St N, motto "all fish and no bull"

horse-and-jockey.text: Pouring pints in South Pasadena since 1987, this traditional English pub does pies, pasties, curries and fish and chips, and is the official Liverpool FC supporters club for Pinellas County, screening every match live.
horse-and-jockey.descriptor: Traditional British pub on Pasadena Ave S since 1987

hubbards-marina.text: Four generations of Hubbards have run this fleet since 1928, when 17-year-old Wilson Hubbard bought five rowboats and 40 cane poles for $150 at Pass-a-Grille. He launched the Gulf Coast's first half-day fishing party boat in 1954, moved the operation to John's Pass in 1976 and opened the Friendly Fisherman restaurant beside it in 1979; today the boats run everything from dolphin cruises to 44-hour offshore trips.
hubbards-marina.descriptor: Family-run fishing and cruise fleet at John's Pass since 1928

hurricane-seafood-restaurant.text: Opened in 1977 on the site of the old Casa Bonita Hotel, itself built where Page's Pavilion bathhouse stood in 1912; the Baltimore-based Falkenstein family bought the hotel's lone surviving remnant and started with a ten-item menu. They added floors in 1986 and 1990, topping it with the Hurricane Watch rooftop bar and its 360-degree sunset views, and the grouper sandwich has been a Pass-a-Grille institution ever since.
hurricane-seafood-restaurant.descriptor: Three-story Pass-a-Grille seafood house with a rooftop sunset bar, since 1977

il-ritorno.text: The name means 'The Return' and marks chef-owner David Benstock's homecoming to St. Pete. In 2025, Pinellas County's first year of Michelin eligibility, it earned a Michelin Guide 'recommended' nod, with no local restaurant receiving a star.
il-ritorno.descriptor: Modern Italian restaurant with a chef's-bar tasting menu at 449 Central Ave

imagine-museum.text: Billionaire philanthropist and glass artist Trish Duggan opened this museum in January 2018 inside a former charter school building on Central Avenue, bankrolling it herself. Its 500-plus-piece core collection was assembled to trace the American Studio Glass movement from the early 1960s onward, and it anchors St. Pete's pitch as Florida's 'Glass Coast' alongside the Chihuly Collection and Duncan McClellan's studio.
imagine-museum.descriptor: Contemporary studio-glass museum at 1901 Central Ave

intermezzo-coffee-cocktails.text: Started around 2016 as a three-month pop-up at 1111 Central Ave by 23-year-old USF St. Pete grad Jarrett Sabatini, modeled on 1950s Roman cafés (marble tables, Boston's Caffé Vittoria). It outlasted its lease by six and a half years, then moved down the block in 2023 into the old Independent Bar space when its original building was slated for a hotel project.
intermezzo-coffee-cocktails.descriptor: EDGE District café by day, craft cocktail bar by night, at 1059 Central Ave

jacks.text: Jack's London Grill is named after the Union Jack, not a person. Surrey-born chef Peter Leonavicius, who moved to Tampa Bay in the 1980s, runs it out of a small building with a patio on 62nd Ave N, and nearly everything, from the fish and chips to the sourdough, is made from scratch.
jacks.descriptor: British pub on 62nd Ave N off 4th St, known for fish and chips

jannus-live.text: Opened in 1984 as Jannus Landing, this open-air courtyard was started to lure reggae and punk shows to Tampa Bay, and is named for pioneering pilot Tony Jannus. The Red Hot Chili Peppers played its first mainstream show in 1987; Green Day, Pearl Jam and Radiohead followed, and it was rebranded Jannus Live after a 2010 reopening.
jannus-live.descriptor: Standing-room outdoor courtyard concert venue downtown since 1984

jimmy-bs-beach-bar.text: It started as a little tiki bar in the early '90s at the 1950s-era Beachcomber resort and grew into a beach bar with live bands two or three times a day, winning Best Florida Beach Bar in 2011, 2012 and 2014–2017. Hurricanes Helene and Milton flooded the property in 2024 with up to four feet of storm surge; it reopened Oct. 30, 2025.
jimmy-bs-beach-bar.descriptor: Beachfront live-music bar at the Beachcomber hotel on Gulf Blvd, St. Pete Beach

joey-brooklyns-famous-pizza.text: Slinging New York-style slices on Jannus Landing, it's the bar district's late-night stop, open until 3 a.m. Thursday through Saturday.
joey-brooklyns-famous-pizza.descriptor: NY-style pizza counter on 1st Ave N by Jannus Live, open till 3 a.m.

jungle-prada-tavern.text: Developer Walter Fuller built the Spanish-Mediterranean Jungle Prada in 1924, naming it after Havana's Paseo del Prado promenade, and its Gangplank club (1925) was St. Pete's first nightclub and a Prohibition speakeasy. Legend says Al Capone owned it, but records show he spent only about two days in town; Babe Ruth really did throw his 1929 wedding reception here during spring training.
jungle-prada-tavern.descriptor: Bar and grill in the 1924 Jungle Prada complex on Boca Ciega Bay

juno-and-the-peacock.text: Opened August 23, 2024 in the extensively renovated, AvroKO-designed space that was 400 Beach Seafood & Tap House (a Beach Drive fixture since 2009). The name comes from Aesop's fable of Juno and the peacock, so expect peacock art (painted and taxidermied) throughout; owners Shawn and Jeanna Damkoehler also run Allelo, and the adjoining Pluma lounge stocks over 1,400 wines.
juno-and-the-peacock.descriptor: Upscale New American coastal restaurant on Beach Drive across from North Straub Park

kahwa-coffee.descriptor: Local-roaster coffee shop with a drive-thru on Park St N near Bay Pines

kahwa-coffee-north.text: Kahwa is St. Pete's homegrown roaster: Sarah and Raphael Perrier founded it in 2006, opened their first downtown café in 2008, and got their big break that same year when chef Paul Bocuse picked Kahwa for his Chefs de France restaurant at Epcot. Today it calls itself Florida's largest independent coffee roaster, with roughly 20 cafés and hundreds of wholesale accounts.
kahwa-coffee-north.descriptor: Local roaster's Downtown North café at 475 2nd St N

kahwa-south.text: The Downtown South café of St. Pete's homegrown roaster, founded in 2006 by Sarah and Raphael Perrier. Kahwa opened its first downtown café in 2008, the same year chef Paul Bocuse chose its beans for his Epcot restaurant, and has since grown into what it bills as Florida's largest independent coffee roaster.
kahwa-south.descriptor: Local roaster's Downtown South café at 204 2nd Ave S

katiki.text: A Sunset Beach locals' bar since 1982 with a palm-thatched tiki hut and live music every day of the week. Hurricanes Helene and Milton in 2024 buried it in sand up to the bottom of the tiki hut and shoved an 800-pound pool table sideways, yet staff dug it out and reopened 21 days after the storm.
katiki.descriptor: Thatched-roof tiki beach bar on Sunset Beach, Treasure Island, live music nightly

kobe-japanese-steakhouse.text: Part of the Florida teppanyaki chain started in 1984 when Doi Tan Nguyen and his son Chau left Montreal and opened the first Kobé in Altamonte Springs near Orlando. Chau took over after his father died in 1996 and grew it into a 13-location family business stretching from Orlando to Tampa Bay, still built around tableside hibachi theatrics like the onion volcano.
kobe-japanese-steakhouse.descriptor: Hibachi/teppanyaki chain restaurant on 66th St N near Tyrone, chain founded 1984

kopper-kitchen.text: A family-run West St. Pete diner going since 1976, the kind of place the Tampa Bay Times called a 40-year stalwart. Everything is made in house, and regulars come for the daily cream puffs and the Boston cream pie as much as the all-day breakfast.
kopper-kitchen.descriptor: Family-owned breakfast-and-lunch diner on Central Ave in West St. Pete since 1976

kress-building.text: Built in 1927 as an S.H. Kress five-and-dime, its parchment-colored terra cotta facade shows the Beaux Arts influence the chain favored. The store closed around 1981, the city used it for offices from 1982 to 1996, and it was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2001.
kress-building.descriptor: 1927 Beaux Arts former five-and-dime at 475 Central Ave, on the National Register

kristinas-cafe.text: A no-frills comfort-food diner on 34th Street North, family owned and operated since 2001, where breakfast runs from open to close alongside country-fried steak and an open-faced roast beef sandwich with mashed potatoes.
kristinas-cafe.descriptor: Family-run all-day-breakfast diner on 34th St N since 2001

la-casa-de-pane.text: An Italian bakeshop that doubles as a small artisanal grocer: sfogliatella, lobster tails, cannoli and fresh focaccia up front, with Italian wines, dried pasta and frozen pizzas on the shelves.
la-casa-de-pane.descriptor: Italian bakery and café on Gulf Blvd in St. Pete Beach

la-teresita.text: Since 1999 the Cortes family has run this Pinellas Park Cuban kitchen, cooking the food they grew up with: roast pork, ropa vieja, pressed Cuban sandwiches and whole fried snapper.
la-teresita.descriptor: Family-run Cuban and Spanish restaurant on 66th St N since 1999

la-v-vietnamese-fusion.text: Open on Central Ave since at least 2016, La V bills its menu as its owners' mother's recipes given a bold, modern twist: a beef pho simmered for 12 hours, and Bun Cha Ha Noi, the Hanoi grilled-pork dish the restaurant calls 'the Anthony Bourdain classic,' alongside house-made boba and Vietnamese coffee.
la-v-vietnamese-fusion.descriptor: Modern Vietnamese restaurant and boba spot at 441 Central Ave downtown

lake-maggiore.text: Settlers called it Salt Lake, a brackish tidal lagoon open to Tampa Bay, until William B. Miranda renamed it in 1883 after the lake on the Swiss-Italian border. A dam built in 1940 cut it off from the bay and turned it into a freshwater lake of about 363 acres, one of the city's largest, later dredged and restored after decades of runoff and algae. Boyd Hill Nature Preserve, whose nature trail was begun in 1947, wraps its southern shore.
lake-maggiore.descriptor: 363-acre lake in south St. Pete, ringed by Boyd Hill Nature Preserve

leverocks.text: Legend says Johnny Leverock won a seven-acre Tampa Bay oyster bed in a poker game, then opened Johnny Leverock's Oyster Bar in Pinellas Park in 1948; the name grew into a multi-restaurant chain across Florida and Georgia before folding in 2006. Longtime operators George Lewis and John Stross revived it here in 2007, a block from the St. Pete Fish House where they started in 1978, and Bertha Leverock's clam chowder and peanut butter pie are still on the menu.
leverocks.descriptor: Old-school seafood house on Pasadena Ave S carrying a 1948 oyster-bar name

lonnis-sandwiches.text: A weekday-lunch institution at 429 Central Avenue since 1987, known for its house Minnesota Wild Rice Bread and the stacked Sunny Bird turkey sandwich. Owner Phillip Ingram bought the shop just before the pandemic and kept it going as the block filled in around it.
lonnis-sandwiches.descriptor: Weekday-only lunch sandwich shop on Central Ave since 1987; Sunny Bird turkey

mandarin-hide.text: Bills itself as St. Pete's original craft-cocktail sanctuary, pouring on Central Avenue for more than 16 years with one of the town's largest spirits collections. Run by four partners, it styles itself a 'cocktail lodge,' and a mascot named Manny has greeted guests since opening night.
mandarin-hide.descriptor: Craft cocktail lodge on the 200 block of Central Ave

mangrove-bay-golf-course.text: City Council approved it in 1975 over inflation-era grumbling, and the course was completed in 1978 on a former landfill for $3 million. By 1990 it drew about 95,000 rounds a year, turned a profit for the city, earned Golf Digest mentions as one of the best public courses in the country, and was the only regulation course in Pinellas that let golfers walk any time, year-round.
mangrove-bay-golf-course.descriptor: City-owned 18-hole, par-72 course on 180 acres off 62nd Ave NE

maple-street-biscuit-company.text: The Jacksonville-born biscuit chain (founded 2012) opened this downtown store on April 4, 2018 in the old Local 662 space after, the founders said, so many St. Pete residents kept asking for one; fans camped out overnight for the opening. The signature Squawking Goat, fried chicken with a fried goat-cheese medallion and pepper jelly on a biscuit, has been featured on Food Network and Travel Channel.
maple-street-biscuit-company.descriptor: Southern biscuit-sandwich breakfast and brunch spot at 662 Central Ave since 2018

mastrys-brewing-co.text: Founder Matthew Dahm is a third-generation Mastry; he named the brewery for his grandmother Juliet Mastry, a former New York City stage singer who ran the original Mastry's Restaurant there. It began as a nano-brewery inside a family member's C.D. Roma restaurant around 2015, moved to Blind Pass Road in August 2016 as St. Pete Beach's first microbrewery, and was ranked the seventh-fastest-growing small brewery in the US in 2017.
mastrys-brewing-co.descriptor: Family-run microbrewery and distillery on Blind Pass Rd, St. Pete Beach, since 2016

maximo-park.text: The largest of the city's four archaeological park sites, it preserves a shell midden left by the Native people who fished where Boca Ciega Bay meets Tampa Bay. It takes its name from Antonio Maximo, who received an 1843 land grant for Seminole War service and ran a fish rancho on the point with William Bunce until the hurricane of 1848 swept their holdings into the Gulf.
maximo-park.descriptor: 70-acre bayfront park with boat ramps, disc golf and a Native shell midden

melt-n-dip.text: A Middle Eastern dessert chain (with shops in Lebanon, Iraq and nearly a dozen across the U.S.) that became a viral phenomenon for over-the-top sweets: three towering chocolate fountains greet you at the door, and the menu runs to Belgian-chocolate crepes, pistachio eclair pyramids and Damascus-style ice cream with keshta. It opened in late 2025 in the old Rollbotto Sushi space.
melt-n-dip.descriptor: Middle Eastern dessert shop on 1st St N, opened 2025 in the former Rollbotto

mi-carreta-restaurant-and-bakery.text: A family-run Colombian restaurant and bakery in Lealman, owned by Marlon Yepes, who immigrated from Medellín. Locals come for the bandeja paisa and the pastry case of tequeños and sweets; in 2024 the family opened a reggaetón nightclub next door because customers kept complaining they had to drive to Tampa for Latin music.
mi-carreta-restaurant-and-bakery.descriptor: Colombian restaurant and bakery on 54th Ave N in Lealman

mickeys-cafe.text: Owner Mickey came from South Africa in 1996 and, after a stint in Key West, opened Central Cafe & Organics in 2005, which he bills as downtown St. Pete's first organic restaurant. This 2014 sequel on Central Avenue follows the same playbook of salads, wraps, house soups, fresh juices and the 'Cosmickey Cookie'.
mickeys-cafe.descriptor: Organic salads, wraps and juices on the 300 block of Central Ave

middle-grounds-grill.text: The Coover family ran this Treasure Island corner as Robbie's Pancake House before remaking it around 2007 as Middle Grounds Grill, an upscale steak-and-seafood spot where a tuxedo or flip-flops are equally welcome. The name comes from the Florida Middle Grounds, the famed fishing banks about 100 miles offshore.
middle-grounds-grill.descriptor: Family-run steak and seafood house on Gulf Blvd, Treasure Island

mirror-lake.text: This was the city's water supply — literally called Reservoir Lake from 1899 — until an Audubon Society member, taken with its glassy surface, got it renamed Mirror Lake in 1915. The park around it holds the city's oldest library (a 1915 Carnegie building) and the St. Petersburg Shuffleboard Club, and in December 2024 the whole lakefront became a local historic district.
mirror-lake.descriptor: Downtown lake park with a 1915 Carnegie library and shuffleboard club

morean-arts-center.text: The Morean traces back to 1917, when Margaret Tadd and her daughter Edith Tadd Little founded the Art Club of St. Petersburg, once billed as the largest art center south of Atlanta. It took the Morean name in 2009 after donor Beth Morean funded the Central Avenue buildings, then in 2010 brought the Chihuly Collection to town, which drew 250,000 visitors in its first five months and now sits across the street at 720 Central.
morean-arts-center.descriptor: Community art center at 719 Central Ave, home to the Chihuly Collection

museum-of-fine-arts.text: St. Petersburg's first art museum, opened in 1965 on a four-acre waterfront site the city donated, thanks to collector Margaret Acheson Stuart, who seeded it with a $1 million endowment and works from her own collection. Its original wing was designed by architect John Volk; the collection now spans some 20,000 objects across nearly 5,000 years.
museum-of-fine-arts.descriptor: Encyclopedic art museum on the Beach Drive waterfront since 1965

neighborhood-joe.text: A mostly vegan neighborhood café known for its vegan BLT (marinated tempeh, avocado, arugula and sprouts) and hard-to-resist blueberry muffins. It closed its original spot just up the block on MLK at the end of December and reopened six weeks later on February 15, 2024, in the plaza next to Trip's Diner, with more patio space.
neighborhood-joe.descriptor: Mostly vegan café and coffee shop on MLK Jr St N next to Trip's Diner

nine-spices-hot-pot.text: Cook-at-the-table hot pot and Korean BBQ where trays of ingredients ride out to you on a conveyor belt, and the kitchen stays open until 1 a.m. every night. A sister Nine Spices now operates in Clearwater on Countryside Blvd.
nine-spices-hot-pot.descriptor: Conveyor-belt hot pot and Korean BBQ on 66th St N in Pinellas Park

nitallys.text: A husband-and-wife Thai-Mexican fusion spot best known for the Inferno Soup Challenge: a 48-ounce, $50 bowl loaded with peppers including ghost chilies. Food Network's Heat Seekers filmed chefs Aaron Sanchez and Roger Mooking attempting it when no one had ever finished; a Gainesville writer eventually conquered it. Nitally's later moved from Central Avenue to 9th Street North.
nitallys.descriptor: Thai-Mex mom-and-pop on 9th St N, home of the Inferno Soup Challenge

north-shore-volleyball-courts.text: Six sand courts on the downtown waterfront at North Shore Park, free on a first-come basis (or rentable), sharing the complex with the North Shore Aquatic Complex pool, tennis courts and a lighted softball field.
north-shore-volleyball-courts.descriptor: Six free beach volleyball courts on the bay at North Shore Park, 901 North Shore Dr NE

north-straub-park.text: Named for William Straub, the St. Petersburg Times editor who crusaded to turn the bayfront into public parkland — the city secured the waterfront lots in 1908–09, a deal the Times called "the best Christmas present St. Petersburg ever had." In the 1920s developer C. Perry Snell shipped some thirty classical statues from Italy for the waterfront parks; only a weathered handful still stand here.
north-straub-park.descriptor: Downtown bayfront lawn with a concert stage on Bayshore Dr NE

nueva-cantina.text: Opened in 2016 by Raul Medina with a kitchen staffed largely by cooks from Mexico City and Jalisco, Nueva Cantina built its reputation on Mexican street food (the birria is the signature) and fresh-squeezed margaritas. The restaurant is now 100% employee-owned and announced a second location in downtown Tampa for 2025.
nueva-cantina.descriptor: Mexican street-food and margarita spot at 1625 4th St S in south St. Pete, since 2016

oak-and-stone.text: Opened July 9, 2018 as the second location of a Sarasota concept, next to the Hyatt Place at the foot of Central. Its claim to fame is the region's largest self-serve beer wall: an RFID wristband unlocks roughly 50 rotating craft taps, bills by the ounce and cuts you off at 40 ounces. Wood-fired pizzas and a 3,000-square-foot deck round it out.
oak-and-stone.descriptor: Wood-fired pizza and self-pour craft beer wall at 199 Central Ave

off-the-brick-new-york-pizza.text: This family-owned pizzeria at 49th St N and 73rd Ave has been baking here since 1999, originally under the name Central Pizza before rebranding as Off The Brick. The dough is still hand-tossed and slid into brick-lined deck ovens on wooden peels, and they run their own delivery drivers instead of third-party apps.
off-the-brick-new-york-pizza.descriptor: NY-style brick-oven pizzeria on 49th St N, since 1999 (ex-Central Pizza)

writtenFor.name: Off The Brick New York Pizza

old-northeast-tavern.text: The Old Northeast's "Cheers" bar sits in a 1925 building that was a WWII servicemen's bar, the N&L Diner, a laundromat and a yoga studio before the tavern opened in 2006. Bob Wareham and Mark Brindle have run it since 2008; it closed in late 2024 to build a shared dining room connecting it to next-door Old Northeast Pizza, and it plans to reopen with a newly acquired liquor license and cocktails for the first time.
old-northeast-tavern.descriptor: Neighborhood pub on 7th Ave N in the Old Northeast, open since 2006

old-southeast-market.descriptor: Corner poke bar, deli and beer market at 3rd St S and 17th Ave in Old Southeast

overflow-brewing-company.text: Sour-beer specialist opened in spring 2018 in a converted office building behind the Morean Arts Center by Troy Bledsoe, a homebrewer-turned-Rapp Brewing brewer, with friends Ryan Sarno and Jessica Holder. Its tap handles were built from Bledsoe's own childhood Legos, some 30 years old. After eight years, it poured its last beers in August 2026.
overflow-brewing-company.descriptor: Sour-focused microbrewery on 1st Ave N with Lego-built tap handles (2018–2026)

oyster-shucker-craft-draft.descriptor: Family-owned waterfront oyster bar with 50+ beers at 650 Corey Ave, St. Pete Beach

pacific-counter.text: This 660 Central storefront is where Pacific Counter started in 2018: three industry veterans (Tanner Loebel, sushi chef Tock Noythanongsay, and Eric Bialik) launched a build-your-own poke bowl and sushi burrito counter that has since grown into a Tampa Bay chain and spent years running a stand at Tropicana Field. Regulars know it for the pineapple soft serve and Spam musubi.
pacific-counter.descriptor: Fast-casual poke bowl and sushi burrito counter on Central Ave, since 2018

paolos-pizza-subs.text: Actually spelled Paulo's, this pizza-and-sub shop has been run by Joe and Maria Santos since 1983. Regulars swear by the sauce and the calzones.
paolos-pizza-subs.descriptor: Family-run pizza and sub shop in St. Petersburg, since 1983

paradise-grille-pass-a-grille.text: This beachfront site held the La Plaza Hotel and then the Pass-a-Grille Hotel, both lost to fire (1922 and 1967), before record producer Phil Gernhard, of 'Snoopy vs. the Red Baron' fame, convinced the city in 1970 to let him build a concession stand so kids would stop crossing the road for sodas. It is still the only concession directly on Pass-a-Grille Beach, and each evening someone rings the old ship's bell at sunset.
paradise-grille-pass-a-grille.descriptor: City-owned beach bar and grill on the sand at Gulf Way, Pass-a-Grille

paradise-grille-upham-beach.text: The sister location of the Pass-a-Grille original, this beach concession sits right on the sand at Upham Beach in St. Pete Beach. Locals still remember the stand by its old name, the Seaside Grille, before it was rebranded; it opens at 7am and closes a half hour past sunset daily.
paradise-grille-upham-beach.descriptor: Beach concession on the sand at Upham Beach, open 7am to past sunset

park-rec.text: Stephen Schrutt's Hunger + Thirst group turned downtown's old World of Beer into a game bar in early 2017: Skee-Ball, air hockey, vintage cabinets from Galaga to Mortal Kombat and a turfed cornhole patio, anchoring a First Avenue S block shared with sister spots The Avenue and Proper. The neon over the bar reads 'youth has no age.'
park-rec.descriptor: Arcade-and-lawn-games bar on 1st Ave S downtown, opened 2017

parkshore-grill.text: Open since 1996, Parkshore Grill bills itself as the first major restaurant on Beach Drive, setting the template for the sidewalk-dining strip that followed. Partner and executive chef Tyson Grant runs the modern American menu, served al fresco with waterfront views.
parkshore-grill.descriptor: Modern American sidewalk-dining restaurant on Beach Drive NE since 1996

perrys-porch.text: Named for C. Perry Snell, the 1920s developer who shaped much of downtown, it opened on the St. Pete Pier in February 2025 in the former Hops & Props space. Owner Ryan Griffin calls it his 'love letter to St. Pete,' down to cocktails named for the Pink Streets and Jungle Prada.
perrys-porch.descriptor: Coastal eatery with a waterfront porch at the St. Pete Pier, opened 2025

pier-teaki.text: The open-air tiki bar on the roof of the Pier head, five floors up at the end of the St. Pete Pier — about as far into Tampa Bay as you can get without getting wet. It sits in the $92 million, 26-acre Pier District that opened July 6, 2020, and is run by the same local owners as Birchwood and The Canopy on Beach Drive.
pier-teaki.descriptor: Rooftop tiki bar on the 5th floor of the St. Pete Pier head

pin-on-grand.text: Opened in the Grand Central District in November 2024 when owners Som and Roger Rattanachane relocated their Pin On Cafe from the EDGE District and refocused it on Thai and northern Laotian cooking — Som is from Thailand, Roger from Laos, and the family previously ran Pin Wok & Bowl and Sab Cafe. Expect Lao-style papaya salad with wild rice noodles alongside sushi stacks, sushi burritos and a full liquor bar.
pin-on-grand.descriptor: Thai and Lao fast-casual with sushi and a full bar, 2458 Central Ave

pin-wok-bowl.text: A Thai-and-Japanese fusion spot on the 400 block of Central, known for sushi burritos and poke bowls alongside pad thai and green curry. Owners Som and Roger Rattanachane went on to open a second concept, Pin On Café, in the Edge District in 2021, staffed almost entirely by relatives and friends.
pin-wok-bowl.descriptor: Thai-Japanese fusion spot on the 400 block of Central Ave (sushi burritos, poke)

pipos.text: The Hernandez family opened the first Pipo's Cuban cafe in Tampa in 1979 and still cooks from the same family recipes at this Bay Pines outpost. Pipo's is a three-time winner of the Ybor Cuban Sandwich Competition and chef-owner Ramon Hernandez a two-time Top Local Chef champ; the roast pork is the house calling card.
pipos.descriptor: Family-run Cuban cafe on Bay Pines Blvd; Tampa roots since 1979

pipos-cuban-cafe.descriptor: Counter-service Cuban cafe on 4th Street N in north St. Pete

poppos-taquiera.text: A family-run taqueria named after the owner's grandfather, "Poppo," that models its burritos and tacos on the Mission District street food of San Francisco — homemade flour and corn tortillas, fresh and organic ingredients, and 12-inch flour-tortilla burritos, served from a storefront at 1033 Central Ave.
poppos-taquiera.descriptor: Cali-style Mexican street food counter at 1033 Central Ave with homemade tortillas

red-white-booze.text: For years this waterfront spot on Pass-a-Grille Way was Sea Critters Cafe, a fixture for boaters and beach vacationers; new owners took it over and rebranded it Red, White & Booze in 2022, keeping the docks, local grouper and margaritas and adding live music on the deck.
red-white-booze.descriptor: Dockside seafood bar on the Intracoastal in Pass-a-Grille, pull up by boat

renzos.text: The downtown flagship of a Tampa-born Argentine steakhouse that started on Kennedy Boulevard in 2009: steaks fired over quebracho wood in a Josper oven, house-made empanadas and a wine list poured from Mendoza outward, a couple of blocks from the Pier.
renzos.descriptor: Argentine steakhouse and wine bar at 2nd St S and 1st Ave S, since 2018

ricks-reef.text: Something has been serving food on this corner since 1939, when Larry's Luncheonette opened as a drive-up hot dog stand; the owners say the original floor is still underfoot. After runs as Capt. Zak's, Spoonbills, Bobby's Place and The Reef, a regular bought the place and reopened it as Rick's Reef in August 2012, keeping the old name.
ricks-reef.descriptor: Casual seafood-and-burger bar on Gulf Blvd at 68th Ave, St. Pete Beach

rococo-steak.text: Opened in October 2013 inside the historic 1920s former YWCA building on 2nd Avenue South. Named for the ornate Rococo art period, it set out to break the idea that a steakhouse is only for special occasions, pairing a modern steak menu with a wine list that has run to more than 600 labels.
rococo-steak.descriptor: Upscale modern steakhouse in the 1920s former YWCA building on 2nd Ave S, opened 2013

rubys-elixir.text: Ruby's grew out of Central Cigars, a cigar shop that opened on Central Avenue in the late 1990s; in 2011 the owners bolted on Ruby's Elixir as a live-music lounge. It now books musicians every night of the week, and the Thursday jazz sessions in its leather-clad "Havana Room" are the local draw.
rubys-elixir.descriptor: Cigar-and-jazz lounge off Central Ave with live music seven nights a week

rumfish-grill-bar.text: The sports-bar half of RumFish Grill at the TradeWinds' RumFish Beach Resort, where the 700-gallon Predator Tank is full of lionfish — the invasive Pacific species the display urges diners to order off the menu to help control. Big-screen TVs, a deck, and the RFG Fish Tank, a 40-ounce cocktail served in a keepsake fishbowl, round it out.
rumfish-grill-bar.descriptor: Sports bar and deck at RumFish Beach Resort with a 700-gallon lionfish tank

rumfish-grill-restaurant.text: You eat beside a 33,500-gallon saltwater aquarium that fills an entire wall — built by Wayde King and Brett Raymer of Acrylic Tank Manufacturing after Guy Harvey and the resort's president challenged them on an hour-long episode of Animal Planet's Tanked. The tank holds Gulf natives like snook, grouper, tarpon and a green moray eel, and the resort even runs a snorkel program that lets guests swim in it.
rumfish-grill-restaurant.descriptor: Seafood restaurant at RumFish Beach Resort with a 33,500-gallon aquarium

saigon-blonde.text: In 2018 St. Pete local Peri Bandazian turned the former LUX lounge at 265 Central into a semi-fictional slice of 1960s Saigon: five rooms of tiki totems and murals by local artist Jean Michael Fait, including a tiny "military bar" built from an old airplane wing and a VIP loft under a muraled ceiling.
saigon-blonde.descriptor: '60s-Saigon tiki cocktail bar at 265 Central Ave, opened 2018

saint-pete-bagel-company.text: Around since 1987, this is the St. Petersburg shop of a small four-store Pinellas chain that hand-rolls New York-style bagels and makes its own donuts, cream cheese and coffee roasts in house; Creative Loafing readers have kept it among Tampa Bay's favorite bagel shops for more than a decade.
saint-pete-bagel-company.descriptor: NY-style bagel and donut bakery on 4th St N, around since 1987

saint-pete-brewing-company.text: Opened in 2014, two years after St. Pete legalized microbreweries. When founder Tom Williams first planned a brewery there were none in the city; by the time his opened it was number five. Flagships St. Pete Orange Wheat and Milo's IPA are canned across Florida's west coast, and in 2021 it took over the storefront next door for an event space called The Nest.
saint-pete-brewing-company.descriptor: Downtown craft brewery on 1st Ave N, home of St. Pete Orange Wheat

sawgrass-lake-park.text: This 400-acre park started life in 1972 as a flood-control project to protect Pinellas Park, and its water-control structure still doubles as natural water treatment for runoff headed to Tampa Bay. The boardwalk runs through one of the largest maple swamps on the Gulf Coast, with an observation tower over the lake, resident alligators, and thousands of migrating birds passing through each spring and fall.
sawgrass-lake-park.descriptor: 400-acre county park with a boardwalk through a maple swamp and a tower

shadracks.text: A red-neon dive in Pass-a-Grille pouring cheap beer since 1972, famously described as a wooden shack turned inside out, with a shingled roof built on the inside. Fishermen, bikers and beach regulars pack it on the first Sunday of every month for the legendary Bloody Mary bar, where you buy the vodka and load a skewer with bacon, meatballs, wings and cheese from the garnish buffet.
shadracks.descriptor: Cash-only dive bar on 8th Ave in Pass-a-Grille since 1972; first-Sunday Bloody Mary bar

shells.text: Shells started in Tampa in 1985 when Swiss chef John Christen bet on fresh seafood at dockside prices over fancy decor; the chain grew to 28 restaurants, and its clam chowder has drawn notice from Gourmet Magazine since 1988. The St. Pete Beach location was revived in 2016 by the founder's son under a 20-foot thatched tiki roof, near where a Shells had first stood around 1990.
shells.descriptor: Casual seafood house with a thatched tiki roof on Gulf Blvd, St. Pete Beach

siam-garden.text: St. Pete's longest-running Thai restaurant, opened in 1988 by chef Piboon "Boone", who learned to cook in Bangkok and bills it as the city's first Thai restaurant back when the cuisine was still a novelty in Tampa Bay. Its signature offer is "Bring Your Catch": hand over the fish you landed (cleaned and fileted) and the kitchen turns it into a multi-course meal with appetizer, soup, entrée and jasmine rice.
siam-garden.descriptor: Thai restaurant on Dr. MLK Jr. St N in Allendale Park, est. 1988

skyway-jacks.text: Founded in 1976 by Jack Thomas as a small shack at O'Neill's Marina feeding commercial boaters and fishermen, the all-day-breakfast joint later moved up to 34th Street South. Look for the giant Humpty Dumpty and rooster out front, and order the scrapple, which the Food Network once crowned Florida's best breakfast dish.
skyway-jacks.descriptor: All-day country breakfast diner on 34th St S since 1976

snappers-sea-grill.text: Fisherman-turned-restaurateur Dan Casey opened Snappers on Valentine's Day 1998 after a dozen years running Dan's Beachside Deli, a business he'd started as a hot dog stand on July 4, 1986 with $86 in first-day sales. Fresh grouper from local fishermen was the deli's calling card, and Casey himself won the King of the Beach fishing tournament in 2017; his son Connor now helps run the place.
snappers-sea-grill.descriptor: Gulf seafood and dry-aged steaks on Gulf Blvd, St. Pete Beach, since 1998

snell-arcade.text: Developer C. Perry Snell filled this 1928 Mediterranean Revival building with tiles and artwork he collected on European trips, running an arcade of imported Italian, Spanish, and Cuban tile from Central Avenue through to the Open Air Post Office. He mortgaged it to fund Snell Isle and lost it in 1933 during the Depression; a planned second tower was never built. The arcade was walled off in 1950, reopened in a 1980s renovation that uncovered an Italian mosaic of Venice's Santa Maria della Salute, and the building became condos in the 2000s.
snell-arcade.descriptor: 1928 Mediterranean Revival landmark at 405 Central Ave, on the National Register

south-straub-park.text: Named for William Straub, the St. Petersburg Times editor who crusaded for years to keep the downtown shoreline as public parkland rather than commercial waterfront. The city announced the land acquisition on Christmas Eve 1909, which his paper called "the best Christmas present that St. Petersburg ever had." The south half now sits beside the Museum of Fine Arts and hosts festivals and art fairs.
south-straub-park.descriptor: Downtown waterfront park lawn beside the Museum of Fine Arts

st-pete-pier.text: St. Pete has had a pier on this spot since 1905's Electric Pier, followed by the 1926 Million Dollar Pier and the inverted-pyramid pier of 1973, which was demolished in 2015. The current 26-acre, $92M Pier District opened in July 2020 with restaurants, Tampa Bay Watch's Discovery Center and Janet Echelman's floating net sculpture Bending Arc.
st-pete-pier.descriptor: 26-acre downtown waterfront pier district on Tampa Bay, opened 2020

st-petersburg-museum-of-history.text: Founded in 1920, this is the oldest museum in Pinellas County; the city gave it the site after the 1921 hurricane wiped out the aquarium that stood there. Its centerpiece is a full-size replica of the Benoist airboat that made the world's first scheduled commercial airline flight, St. Petersburg to Tampa, on January 1, 1914, and it also holds Little Cooperstown, the largest collection of signed baseballs in the world.
st-petersburg-museum-of-history.descriptor: City history museum on 2nd Ave NE, home to the 1914 first-airline Benoist replica

stillwaters-tavern.text: Opened in June 2015 in the old Bruce Watters Jewelers space on Beach Drive by the group behind BellaBrava a few doors down. The opening menu was built by Top Chef season 10 alum Jeffrey Jew, and the kitchen still sells itself as a from-scratch American tavern leaning on local fish, farms and regional craft beer.
stillwaters-tavern.descriptor: American scratch kitchen and bar on Beach Drive since 2015

sunken-gardens.text: A century-old botanical garden that began as a sinkhole: plumber George Turner Sr. bought the lot in 1903, drained its shallow lake, and found the rich muck grew just about anything. He started charging a nickel for tours in the 1930s, and the city bought the gardens in 1999 to save them from redevelopment — today it's four acres of tropical plants, flamingos, and one of St. Pete's oldest roadside attractions.

sushi-sho-rexley.text: Brought omakase to downtown St. Pete in January 2018, when brothers Arte and Rexley Kwok, who previously ran Lazy Maguro in Palm Harbor, opened it near 2nd Street North. Chef Rexley, trained under master sushi chef Hiro Ida and making sushi in the area since 1999, serves a chef's-choice progression of up to a dozen courses in an 800-square-foot room; it holds a MICHELIN Recommended listing, retained in the 2026 guide.
sushi-sho-rexley.descriptor: Omakase sushi counter on 2nd St N, open since 2018

tampa-bay-watch-discovery-center.text: The nonprofit Tampa Bay Watch's marine education center at the St. Pete Pier, opened alongside the new Pier in 2020. Touch tanks, a wet lab, and exhibits on the bay's oysters, seagrass, and sea life make it the science stop on a Pier walk.

ted-peters-smoked-fish.text: Ted Peters found a discarded smoker just after World War II and put it out front by the road so people could see and smell it; the family has been smoking mullet, mackerel, mahi and salmon over red oak in the same brown wooden building on Pasadena Ave since around 1950. Still cash-only, still open-air picnic tables, still run by the founder's descendants, with the German potato salad recipe from 'Mom' Tilla Lathrop.
ted-peters-smoked-fish.descriptor: Open-air smoked-fish shack on Pasadena Ave since 1950, cash only

tequila-daisy.text: Opened July 1, 2023 by Monique Grespan and Melissa Powell (also a partner in nearby Pour Judgement), who planned a 100-150 bottle collection and ended up with more than 500 tequilas and agave spirits, one of the largest tequila bars in the U.S. The name nods to the margarita's origin story: "margarita" means "daisy," and legend says the drink was born when a bartender grabbed tequila instead of brandy for a Brandy Daisy.
tequila-daisy.descriptor: Bright tequila-and-mezcal cocktail bar on 1st Ave N, opened 2023

thai-am.text: One of St. Pete's oldest Thai restaurants, a 4th Street North fixture for more than 20 years, run by a Thai-born owner and head chef cooking with ingredients imported from Thailand. The showpiece is Chicken on Fire (gai fai), a fried chicken breast in spicy chili sauce that arrives flaming with whiskey; the cheese-stuffed tempura chicken wings are the other local favorite.
thai-am.descriptor: Family-run Thai restaurant at 6040 4th St N, a fixture for 20+ years

the-ale-and-the-witch.text: This taphouse opened in early 2011 under Brett Andress with a single rule: every tap pours American craft beer, 32 of them at launch. Tucked in the Tower Plaza courtyard between Beach Drive and BayWalk, it has hosted live local music in its courtyard for over a decade and is beloved as one of downtown's craft-beer third places.
the-ale-and-the-witch.descriptor: American craft beer taphouse in the Tower Plaza courtyard off Beach Drive

the-bends.text: Opened in 2012 and billing itself as a "classy dive bar," The Bends is St. Pete's go-to spot for cheap drinks and free live shows, with local and touring bands and monthly DJ residencies packing a back room that I Love the Burg called "a secret portal to the underground."
